promptHead: Athlete goal: 5K (Corrowmore Harvest 5K) on Sun Nov 15 2026, 10 weeks out, target run the whole way.

new.headline: A strong first week, and no pain. Keep to three runs a week, slow the running parts to a pace where you can talk, and make them a little longer each time. That is the surest way to run the whole 5K.

flags.title: How hard the running feels
flags.detail: your running parts felt 6–7/10, with a quarter of the time in zone 3. Slow them until you can talk easily, effort 5/10 or less.

flags.title: Calf tightness
flags.detail: tight the day after a run and gone by next morning is normal. If it lasts longer or turns into pain, repeat this week and don't move up.

flags.title: Saturday's step
flags.detail: only move to 2-minute runs if Monday and Wednesday felt 6/10 or easier. If not, repeat Monday's session.

flags.title: Rest days
flags.detail: keep runs to Monday, Wednesday and Saturday. Your legs get stronger on the days between runs, so don't fill those days with running.

answers.question: I want to be ready for the 5K in November. Should I run every day next week to get there faster?
answers.answer:
No. Keep to three runs a week, with a day off running between each one. Your heart and lungs get fitter quickly. Your calves, tendons and bones take longer, and they get stronger on the days between runs. The calf tightness you feel the day after each run shows they are already working hard.

Running every day would raise your risk of a niggle that costs you weeks, and that is how people really fall behind. Ten weeks of three steady runs is enough to go from walk-run to running the whole 5K. Your dog walks on the other days already help, so keep them going.

new.analysis:
This was a solid start: three walk-runs on the planned days, all finished, with no pain. Your pace and heart rate were very steady from start to finish, and your heart rate barely crept up. On Saturday you already took a step, stretching the running parts from 1 minute to 1 minute 30.

**The one thing to change is how hard the running parts feel.** They felt 6–7/10, and a quarter of your time was in zone 3, which is more effort than you need. To run 5K without stopping, what counts is time spent running, not speed. A slower jog lets you run for longer, sooner.

**There are no fast sessions in the plan, even though this stage of training is called "build".** For a new runner, building means making the running parts longer. Your goal is to run the whole way, not to hit a time. So every run stays easy, and two short strength sessions help your legs cope with the running.

**This week settles in before it steps up.** Monday and Wednesday repeat Saturday's pattern so it starts to feel normal. Saturday's session is the same length, but the running parts are longer. Your running time goes from 28 minutes last week to about 36 minutes.

**This is the rough path to race day.** I will adjust it each week depending on how you feel.

| Weeks | Running parts |
| --- | --- |
| Aug 31 – Sep 6 | 1.5 to 2 min |
| Sep 7 – 20 | 3 to 5 min |
| Sep 21 – 27 | Lighter week, no step up |
| Sep 28 – Oct 11 | 8 to 12 min |
| Oct 12 – 25 | 15 to 25 min |
| Oct 26 – Nov 8 | 30 to 40 min without stopping |
| Nov 9 – 15 | Lighter week, race Sun Nov 15 |

**Each step comes only when the last one felt comfortable.** Repeating a week is normal and not a setback. About 40 minutes of gentle jogging covers 5 km, so that is what we are working towards.
